title: Collecting and Organising Data: Tally Marks and Tables
seo_title: Grade 4 Collecting and Organising Data Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
standard_text: Collect data using tally marks and tables for recording; order data from smallest group to largest group; sort, group and organise data in tables.
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 4 data handling worksheets: tally marks, tally tables, organising and comparing data. 100 questions with memos.
key_big: A gate of tally marks is 5.
key_sub: Organise data in a table to compare.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • To collect data, ask a question and record each answer.
  • Use tally marks: draw 4 lines and cross them with the 5th to make a group of 5.
  • Count the tallies in groups of 5 and write the total in a table.
  • Organise data in a table so it is easy to compare.

Examples

Example

Tally: two gates and 3 more

5 + 5 + 3

Answer: 13

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
A gate as 4A gate (4 lines crossed) is 5.
Counting twiceCross out each answer as you tally it.
Adding for how many moreSubtract to compare.

faq.q: What does CAPS Grade 4 say about collecting data?
faq.a: Collect data using tally marks and tables for recording, and order data from smallest group to largest group.

faq.q: Why group tally marks in fives?
faq.a: Groups of 5 are quick to count.
A table showing how often each answer occurs.

faq.q: What makes a good survey question?
faq.a: A clear question with clear answer choices.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 3 groups of 5 and 3 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 3 = 18.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 5 groups of 5 and 2 more: 5 × 5 = 25, and 25 + 2 = 27.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 6 groups of 5 and 4 more: 6 × 5 = 30, and 30 + 4 = 34.
Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 8 groups of 5 and 1 more: 8 × 5 = 40, and 40 + 1 = 41.
23 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 3, so look for 4 groups of 5 and 3 single marks. That is C. A shows 28 (one group of 5 too many); B shows 22 (one single mark is missing); D shows 24 (one single mark too many).

items.q: What number should go in the Frequency column for Mango?
items.e: The frequency is the number the tally marks show. Mango has 3 groups of 5 and 1 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 1 = 16.

items.q: Which fruit got the fewest votes?
items.e: Orange has the shortest tally: 1 group of 5 and 1 more, so 6 votes. Apple has 8, the next fewest.

items.q: How many more votes did Mango get than Watermelon?
items.e: Mango 16 (3 groups of 5 and 1 more). Watermelon 11. How many more means subtract: 16 − 11 = 5. (Counting each tally group as 4 makes Mango 13, and 13 − 11 = 2.)

items.q: Every learner in 4B voted once. How many learners are in 4B?
items.e: Find the Mango frequency first: 16. Then add all the rows: 8 + 13 + 16 + 6 + 11 = 54.

items.q: How many learners have 2 pets?
items.e: Find the row for 2 pets. The frequency is 7, so 7 learners have 2 pets. The 2 is the number of pets, not the number of learners.

items.q: What is the most common number of pets?
items.e: The biggest frequency is 9, in the row for 1 pet. So 1 pet is the most common answer. 9 is how many learners, not how many pets.

items.q: How many learners answered the survey?
items.e: Add the frequencies: 5 + 9 + 7 + 3 + 2 = 26 learners. (10 adds the numbers of pets, 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4. 21 leaves out the learners with no pets.)

items.q: Favourite colour (frequency table): Red 5, Blue 8, Pink 3, Grey 6. Which bar graph shows the same data?
items.e: C matches every number (the scale goes up in 1s). A: two columns are the wrong way round; B: one column is one line too high; D: one column is one line too low.

items.q: People in families (frequency table): 2 people: 4, 3 people: 9, 4 people: 12, 5 people: 7. Which bar graph shows the same data?
items.e: A matches every number (the scale goes up in 2s). B: two columns are the wrong way round; C: a column is on the line below (it should be halfway between two lines); D: one column is one line too high.

items.q: Cans collected (frequency table): 3A 25, 3B 40, 3C 15, 3D 30. Which bar graph shows the same data?
items.e: D matches every number (the scale goes up in 5s). A: two columns are the wrong way round; B: one column is one line too high; C: one column is one line too low.

items.q: Ice blocks sold (frequency table): Mon 11, Tue 6, Wed 14, Thu 9. Which bar graph shows the same data?
items.e: B matches every number (the scale goes up in 2s). A: two columns are the wrong way round; C: a column is on the line below (it should be halfway between two lines); D: one column is one line too high.
First count the tallies: Dog 6, Cat 4, Fish 3, Bird 5. B matches every number (each symbol = 1). A: two rows are the wrong way round; C: one row has a symbol too many; D: one row is missing a symbol.
D matches every number (each symbol = 2). A: two rows are the wrong way round; B: a half symbol is drawn as a whole symbol; C: one row has a symbol too many.
A matches every number (each symbol = 5). B: two rows are the wrong way round; C: one row has a symbol too many; D: one row is missing a symbol.

First count the tallies: Apple 10, Kiwi 7, Plum 12, Pear 5. C matches every number (each symbol = 2). A: two rows are the wrong way round; B: a half symbol is drawn as a whole symbol; D: one row has a symbol too many.

items.q: How many vans went past the school?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Van row has 2 groups of 5 and 2 more: 2 × 5 = 10, and 10 + 2 = 12.

items.q: How many cars went past the school?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Car row has 1 group of 5 and 1 more: 1 × 5 = 5, and 5 + 1 = 6.

items.q: How many sparrows were seen?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Sparrow row has 3 groups of 5 and 4 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 4 = 19.

items.q: Which row shows 11 birds?
items.e: 11 = 5 + 5 + 1. Look for 2 groups of 5 and 1 single mark. That is the Robin row.

items.q: How many black cars were there?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Black row has 1 group of 5 and 4 more: 1 × 5 = 5, and 5 + 4 = 9.

items.q: How many cars are shown in the tally chart altogether?
items.e: Count each row: Black 9, White 14, Silver 5, Red 11. Then add: 9 + 14 + 5 + 11 = 39 cars.

items.q: How many votes did Grapes get?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Grapes row has 3 groups of 5 and 2 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 2 = 17.

items.q: What is the difference between the biggest and the smallest number of votes?
items.e: The biggest is Banana (20). The smallest is Pear (11). Difference means subtract: 20 − 11 = 9.

items.q: Which row shows 6 learners?
items.e: 6 = 5 + 1. Look for 1 group of 5 and 1 single mark. That is the Netball row.

items.q: How many learners are shown in the tally chart altogether?
items.e: Count each row: Soccer 15, Netball 6, Swimming 13, Cricket 11. Then add: 15 + 6 + 13 + 11 = 45 learners.

items.q: How many books did Grade 4 borrow on Monday?
items.e: Find the Monday row, then go across to the Grade 4 column. The cell says 34.

items.q: How many books were borrowed on Thursday altogether?
items.e: Add the two cells in the Thursday row: 18 + 25 = 43.

items.q: On which day were the most books borrowed altogether?
items.e: Add each row: Mon 55, Tue 46, Wed 36, Thu 43. The biggest total is 55 on Monday.

items.q: How many books did Grade 3 borrow on Monday?
items.e: Find the Monday row, then go across to the Grade 3 column. The cell says 15.

items.q: How many books did Grade 3 borrow from Monday to Thursday?
items.e: Add the whole Grade 3 column: 15 + 26 + 28 + 22 = 91.

items.q: How many books did Grade 3 borrow on Thursday?
items.e: Find the Thursday row, then go across to the Grade 3 column. The cell says 25.

items.q: How many books were borrowed on Monday altogether?
items.e: Add the two cells in the Monday row: 22 + 11 = 33.

items.q: How many books did Grade 4 borrow from Monday to Thursday?
items.e: Add the whole Grade 4 column: 11 + 35 + 23 + 28 = 97.

items.q: How many cars went past the school?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Car row has 4 groups of 5 and 2 more: 4 × 5 = 20, and 20 + 2 = 22.

items.q: How many buses went past the school?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. The Bus row has 3 groups of 5 and 2 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 2 = 17.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 1 group of 5 and 3 more: 1 × 5 = 5, and 5 + 3 = 8.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 2 groups of 5 and 3 more: 2 × 5 = 10, and 10 + 3 = 13.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 3 groups of 5 and 4 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 4 = 19.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 4 groups of 5 and 2 more: 4 × 5 = 20, and 20 + 2 = 22.
16 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 1, so look for 3 groups of 5 and 1 single mark. That is B. A shows 21 (one group of 5 too many); C shows 15 (one single mark is missing); D shows 17 (one single mark too many).

items.q: What number should go in the Frequency column for Mango?
items.e: The frequency is the number the tally marks show. Mango has 2 groups of 5 and 4 more: 2 × 5 = 10, and 10 + 4 = 14.

items.q: Which fruit got the most votes?
items.e: Mango has 14 votes (2 groups of 5 and 4 more). That is more than Watermelon (11) and Apple (9).

items.q: How many more votes did Watermelon get than Orange?
items.e: Watermelon 11, Orange 4. How many more means find the difference: 11 − 4 = 7.

items.q: How many learners voted altogether? (Each learner voted once.)
items.e: Find the Mango frequency first: 14. Then add all the rows: 9 + 6 + 14 + 4 + 11 = 44.

items.q: How many families have 4 people?
items.e: Find the row for 4 people. The frequency is 11 (2 groups of 5 and 1 more). The 4 is the number of people, not the number of families.

items.q: Which number of people is the most common family size?
items.e: The biggest frequency is 11, in the row for 4 people. So 4 people is the most common family size. 11 is how many families, not how many people.

items.q: How many families are in the survey?
items.e: Add the frequencies: 3 + 7 + 11 + 5 + 2 = 28 families. (20 is 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6, the family sizes.)

items.q: Grade 4 want to collect 200 cans for the food bank. How many more cans do they need?
items.e: Step 1: cans so far: 40 + 25 + 55 + 30 = 150. Step 2: 200 − 150 = 50. (Reading the 4B bar as 20 or 30 gives a wrong total.)
Each star = 4 books, so half a star = 2. Zinhle: 3 × 4 + 2 = 14. Thandi: 2 × 4 + 2 = 10. Altogether means add: 14 + 10 = 24.

items.q: How many more cakes were sold on Friday than on Monday?
items.e: Each circle = 10 cakes, so half a circle = 5. Friday: 5 × 10 = 50. Monday: 2 × 10 + 5 = 25. How many more means subtract: 50 − 25 = 25.

items.q: How many tickets were sold altogether?
items.e: Add all four cells: 46 + 38 = 84 on Thursday and 62 + 54 = 116 on Friday. 84 + 116 = 200.

items.q: How many more cars went past than buses and lorries together?
items.e: Cars: 4 groups of 5 and 3 more = 23. Buses and lorries together: 7 + 9 = 16. Difference: 23 − 16 = 7.

items.q: The chart shows all 30 days of April. The class played outside at lunchtime on every day that was not rainy. On how many days did they play outside?
items.e: Step 1: the Rainy bar ends on the line for 8, so 8 days were rainy. Step 2: 30 − 8 = 22 days. Check: 12 + 7 + 3 = 22.

items.q: The journey to the seaside is 80 km. How much further did the car still have to go at 10:30?
items.e: At 10:30 the point is on the line for 30, so the car had travelled 30 km. Still to go: 80 − 30 = 50 km.

items.q: How much warmer was the warmest time of the day than 09:00?
items.e: The warmest point is 16 °C at 13:00. At 09:00 it was 7 °C. Difference: 16 − 7 = 9 °C.

items.q: Ofentse will draw a pictograph of these votes: 40, 25, 35 and 50. She wants whole symbols only, and as few symbols as she can. Which key should she use?
items.e: Every number is in the 5 times table, so a key of 5 gives whole symbols: 8, 5, 7 and 10. A key of 10 or 2 would need half symbols for 25 and 35. A key of 1 needs 150 symbols.

items.q: Pieter will draw a pictograph of 60, 90, 40 and 70 learners. He wants whole symbols only, and as few symbols as he can. Which key should he use?
items.e: Every number is a multiple of 10, so a key of 10 gives whole symbols: 6, 9, 4 and 7 (26 symbols). A key of 5 also works, but it needs twice as many symbols (52).

items.q: Ethan will draw a bar graph of 12, 18, 6 and 14 votes. Every column must end exactly on a gridline, and he wants no more than 10 gridlines above 0. What should the scale go up in?
items.e: Counting in 1s needs 18 gridlines, which is too many. Counting in 2s needs 9 gridlines (2 to 18), and every number is even, so every column ends on a line. In 5s or 10s, 12, 18, 6 and 14 would end between lines.

items.q: Thandi will draw a bar graph of 35, 50, 20 and 45 tickets. Every column must end exactly on a gridline, and she wants no more than 10 gridlines above 0. What should the scale go up in?
items.e: Counting in 5s needs 10 gridlines (5 to 50), and every number is in the 5 times table. 1s or 2s need far too many lines (50 or 25). In 10s, 35 and 45 would end halfway between lines.

items.q: Raffle tickets sold (frequency table): 4A 45, 4B 70, 4C 30, 4D 55. Which bar graph shows the same data?
items.e: C matches every number (the scale goes up in 10s). A: two columns are the wrong way round; B: a column is on the line below (it should be halfway between two lines); D: one column is one line too high.

items.q: Ice blocks sold (frequency table): Mon 20, Tue 30, Wed 15, Thu 25. Which pictograph shows the same data?
items.e: A matches every number (each symbol = 5). B: two rows are the wrong way round; C: one row has a symbol too many; D: one row is missing a symbol.
D matches every number (each symbol = 10). A: two rows are the wrong way round; B: a half symbol is drawn as a whole symbol; C: one row has a symbol too many.

items.q: The pictograph and the bar graph show the same data. How many tickets should the missing 4C column show?
items.e: Read the 4C row of the pictograph. Each circle = 10 tickets. The 4C row has 3 circles and half a circle: 3 × 10 = 30, and half of 10 is 5, so 30 + 5 = 35 tickets. Draw the 4C column up to 35.
Read the Thandi row of the pictograph. Each star = 2 books. The Thandi row has 4 stars and half a star: 4 × 2 = 8, and half of 2 is 1, so 8 + 1 = 9 books. Draw the Thandi column up to 9.

items.q: How many learners read 3 books?
items.e: Each dot is one learner. Count the dots above 3: there are 5. (3 is the number of books, not the number of learners.)

items.q: How many learners are shown on the dot plot?
items.e: Each dot is one learner, so count every dot: 2 + 4 + 6 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 23. (7 counts the stacks, and 28 adds the numbers on the line.)

items.q: What is the most common number of books read?
items.e: The tallest stack of dots is above 2 (6 dots). So 2 books is the most common answer. 6 is how many learners, not how many books.

items.q: How many learners read more than 4 books?
items.e: More than 4 means 5, 6 or 7 books. There are 2 dots above 5, none above 6 and 1 above 7: 2 + 1 = 3. (6 also counts the learners who read exactly 4.)

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: The same number of learners read 2 books and 3 books.
More learners read 1 book than 5 books.
Every learner read at least 1 book.
items.e: 1 book has 4 dots and 5 books has 2 dots, so this is true. Only 1 learner read 7 books. 2 learners read 0 books. 2 books has 6 dots and 3 books has 5.

items.q: How many learners have no brothers or sisters?
items.e: No brothers or sisters means the answer 0. There are 4 dots above 0.

items.q: How many learners have 2 or more brothers and sisters?
items.e: 2 or more means 2, 3, 4 or 5: 6 + 3 + 0 + 2 = 11. (5 leaves out the learners with exactly 2.)

items.q: How many more learners have 1 brother or sister than have 3?
items.e: Above 1 there are 9 dots. Above 3 there are 3 dots. 9 − 3 = 6. (2 is 3 − 1, the numbers on the line, not the dots.)

items.q: Palesa asked 4A, “How many brothers and sisters do you have?” She wants to show each answer as one dot above a number line. Which display should she use?
items.e: A dot plot has a number line, and each answer is one dot above its number. It suits numerical data such as 0, 1, 2 or 3 brothers and sisters.

items.q: Ethan says Graph B shows fewer cans than Graph A because its columns are shorter. Is he right?
c: No. Graph B shows more cans.
No. Both graphs show the same numbers.
Yes. The columns in Graph B are shorter.
Yes. Graph B has fewer gridlines.
items.e: Graph A goes up in 5s and Graph B goes up in 10s. Read both: 4A 20, 4B 35, 4C 40, 4D 25. The numbers are the same; only the scale is different. Always read the scale, not the height.

items.q: Read Graph B. How many cans did 4B collect?
items.e: Graph B goes up in 10s. The 4B column ends halfway between 30 and 40, so it shows 35. (3 counts the grid spaces. Graph A shows 35 too.)

items.q: Thabo says, “Twice as many learners chose AFL as chose swimming.” Is he right?
c: Yes. AFL is the most popular sport.
No. AFL got 5 and swimming got 2.
No. Twice 10 is 20, but AFL got 25.
Yes. AFL got 25 and swimming got 10.
items.e: Swimming 10, AFL 25. Twice 10 is 20, and 25 is more than 20, so he is not right. (5 and 2 are grid spaces, not learners.)

items.q: How many learners come to school by car?
items.e: Each circle stands for 10 learners. The Car row has 8 circles: 8 × 10 = 80. (8 reads each circle as 1 learner.)

items.q: How many more learners come by car than walk?
items.e: Car: 8 circles = 80. Walk: 4 circles and half a circle = 40 + 5 = 45. 80 − 45 = 35. (Leaving out the half circle gives 80 − 40 = 40.)

items.q: How many learners walk, ride a bike or ride a scooter?
items.e: Walk 45, Bike 20, Scooter 15 (1 circle and half a circle). 45 + 20 + 15 = 80. (Leaving out the half circles gives 40 + 20 + 10 = 70. 8 counts the circles.)

items.q: Next term, 20 learners who come by car will walk instead. What should the Walk row show then?
items.e: Walk now: 45. 45 + 20 = 65 learners. 65 = 60 + 5: 6 circles for 60 and half a circle for 5.

items.q: Which conclusion is supported by the pictograph?
c: More learners come by car than walk and ride a scooter together.
No learners come to school by train.
The bus is the least common way to travel.
items.e: Car 80. Walk and scooter: 45 + 15 = 60. 80 is more, so this is supported. Walking (45) is not most of the 195 learners. Train was not in the survey, so we cannot tell. Scooter (15) is the least common.

items.q: How many learners read at least 3 books?
items.e: At least 3 means 3, 4 or 5 books: 6 + 3 + 1 = 10 learners. (4 leaves out the learners who read exactly 3. 21 is the learners who read 3 or fewer.)

items.q: How many books did these learners read altogether?
items.e: Multiply each number of books by its frequency: 0 × 2 + 1 × 5 + 2 × 8 + 3 × 6 + 4 × 3 + 5 × 1 = 0 + 5 + 16 + 18 + 12 + 5 = 56. (25 is the number of learners, and 15 adds 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5.)

items.q: Which conclusion is supported by the table?
c: Every learner in 4D read at least one book.
Most learners in 4D read 2 or 3 books.
4D read more books than every other class.
Nobody read 6 books because the books were too long.
items.e: 2 or 3 books: 8 + 6 = 14 of the 25 learners, which is more than half. 2 learners read 0 books. The table has no data about other classes, and it does not tell us why.

items.q: The teacher says, “More than half the class read 2 or more books.” Is she right?
c: No. 7 learners read fewer than 2 books.
items.e: 2 or more books: 8 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 18 learners. Half of 25 is 12 and a half, and 18 is more, so she is right.

items.q: How many learners chose AFL or soccer?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. AFL ends on 12. Soccer ends halfway between 8 and 10, so 9. AFL or soccer means add: 12 + 9 = 21. (Reading soccer as 8 gives 20.)

items.q: Every learner in Grade 3 voted once. How many learners voted?
items.e: Read every column: 12, 7, 10, 9 and 4. Cricket and soccer end between gridlines, so they are 7 and 9. 12 + 7 + 10 + 9 + 4 = 42. (Reading 7 and 9 as 6 and 8 gives 40.)

items.q: How many pieces of fruit were eaten at break altogether?
items.e: Each circle = 2, so half a circle = 1. Apple 8, banana 5 × 2 + 1 = 11, mango 6, orange 2 × 2 + 1 = 5. 8 + 11 + 6 + 5 = 30. (Counting the circles gives 16. Leaving out the halves gives 28.)

items.q: How many more bananas than oranges were eaten?
items.e: Banana 11, orange 5. How many more means subtract: 11 − 5 = 6. (3 is the difference in the number of circles, not in pieces of fruit.)

items.q: How many learners do not come to school by car?
items.e: Not by car means walk, bus or bike: 9 + 6 + 3 = 18. (32 is everyone, and 14 is only the car learners.)

items.q: Next week 5 of the car learners will walk instead. How many learners will walk?
items.e: 5 more learners will walk: 9 + 5 = 14. (19 adds the 5 to the car row instead.)

items.q: What is the most common number of people in a family?
items.e: The tallest column is above 4, so 4 people is the most common. The column is 8 high, which means 8 families, not 8 people.

items.q: How many families have 5 or more people?
items.e: 5 or more means the columns for 5 and 6 people: 4 + 2 = 6 families. (11 adds the family sizes 5 + 6, not the families.)

items.q: How many families were in the survey?
items.e: Add the heights of all the columns: 3 + 6 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 23 families. (20 adds the numbers under the columns, 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6.)

items.q: Grade 3 wants to collect 150 cans. How many more cans do they need?
items.e: Each square = 5 cans. 3A 30, 3B 45, 3C 20, 3D 35. Step 1: 30 + 45 + 20 + 35 = 130. Step 2: 150 − 130 = 20. (Counting squares gives 26, and 150 − 26 = 124.)
